title: Should you lock out your lifts?
summary: NH argues that lockout and depth standards come from competition judging, not hypertrophy. Lockout is where the skeleton holds the load and muscles are least engaged, so for bodybuilding it adds little and repeated locking can wear joints. Lock out only when you can do so painlessly every week. Full range at the bottom matters for injury prevention, while lockout strength never needs training.
claims: Lockout and depth standards exist to standardize judging in powerlifting and Olympic lifting, not for hypertrophy
Many lifters lock out or hit specific depth only because of pressure from the form police
At lockout the joints are aligned and the skeleton holds the weight, so muscles are least engaged; that is why competition judges at the top
You can hold a max deadlift at lockout until your grip fails; with straps, the thoracic spine gives first, then the lumbar spine, then the posterior chain
When a deadlift fails, the thoracic spine tends to give first, then the lumbar, then the hips shoot up
For powerlifting, locking out reduces injury risk, but for bodybuilding the goal is to take the skeleton out of the lift
Locking the knees once is harmless for a 1RM, but locking after every rep over many reps can wear the knee down
Going all the way down on a curl to full extension disengages the biceps and loads the tendon; bouncing out of that stretch on the tendon is dangerous
At the bottom of a squat the knees are deloaded and stress shifts to the lumbar and glutes; at the bottom of a bench the shoulders and pecs are stretched
Whether to lock out depends on the lift and on how your body handles it
NH locks his knees on squats because it has never hurt him, but sometimes skips it to keep tension on the quads
Constant tension is a weak argument against locking out because the tonnage gained at the top, where the quads are nearly disengaged, is negligible
Good reasons not to lock out are that it throws off your technique, kills your groove, or hurts
If you can lock out consistently week after week without pain, lock out
On the deadlift, failing to lock out properly and faking it by pushing the hips forward from a poor setup is what creates pain, not the lockout itself
A straight, neutral-back locked deadlift with the head facing forward is the strongest position and NH has never heard of anyone getting hurt there
Many people, including NH, get elbow tendonitis from locking out every bench rep, so he never locks his elbows on bench
On the overhead press, lock the shoulders so the bar finishes above the head, not in front, which develops all three delt heads; locking the elbows adds nothing
The final few degrees of elbow lockout represent around 2% of triceps activation on the overhead press
The claim that not locking out creates a dangerous strength imbalance is false because you are never forced into lockout under load
NH prescribes full range at the bottom of lifts for injury prevention: a failed rep can force you deep, where you are weakest and can snap something
Full range of motion is better for hypertrophy
The body is strongest at lockout, so lockout needs no practice; you practice it anyway when unracking a bench or squat
Unless you compete in Olympic weightlifting, you do not need to lock the elbows overhead; just push your head through the window and lock the shoulders
For every practice in your bodybuilding training, ask why you do it; if you cannot answer, you probably succumbed to peer pressure
exercises: locking knees optional; lock if pain-free
constant locking under many reps can wear the knee
do not go to full elbow extension or bounce off the tendon
bottom stretch loads the tendon, not the biceps
NH does not lock the elbows
locking every rep can cause elbow tendonitis
lock the shoulders, bar above head, head through the window; elbow lockout not needed
develops all three delt heads; elbow lockout adds ~2% triceps work
finish fully locked with neutral back, head forward; don't fake lockout by pushing hips
